Exponential Attractor for Hindmarsh-Rose Equations in Neurodynamics

Chi Phan Address: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of South Florida, Tampa, FL 33620, USA Email address: chi@mail.usf.edu and Yuncheng You Address: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of South Florida, Tampa, FL 33620, USA Email address: you@mail.usf.edu
Date: August 14, 2019
Abstract.

The existence of an exponential attractor for the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations on a three-dimensional bounded domain originated in the study of neurodynamics is proved through uniform estimates together with a new theorem on the squeezing property of an abstract reaction-diffusion equation also proved in this paper. The results infer that the global attractor whose existence has been established in [23] for the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow has a finite fractal dimension.

Key words and phrases: 
Hindmarsh-Rose equations, exponential attractor, squeezing property, asymptotic compactness, finite fractal dimension
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 35B41, 35K57, 37L30, 37L55; Secondary: 37N25, 92C20

1. Introduction

The Hindmarsh-Rose equations for neuronal spiking-bursting of the intracellular membrane potential observed in experiments was originally proposed in [14, 15]. This mathematical model composed of three coupled ordinary differential equations has been studied through numerical simulations and mathematical analysis in recent years, cf. [14, 15, 17, 21, 30, 39] and the references therein.

We shall study in this paper the global dynamics in terms of the existence of an exponential attractor for the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations:

(1.1) ∂u∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} =d1​Δ​u+φ⁡(u)+v−w+J,\displaystyle=d_{1}\Delta u+\varphi(u)+v-w+J,\,
(1.2) ∂v∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} =d2​Δ​v+ψ⁡(u)−v,\displaystyle=d_{2}\Delta v+\psi(u)-v,
(1.3) ∂w∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial w}{\partial t} =d3​Δ​w+q⁡(u−c)−r​w,\displaystyle=d_{3}\Delta w+q(u-c)-rw,

for t>0,x∈Ω⊂ℝnt>0,\;x\in\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (n≤3n\leq 3), where Ω\Omega is a bounded domain with locally Lipschitz continuous boundary, JJ is a constant and the nonlinear terms

(1.4) φ⁡(u)=a​u2−b​u3,andψ⁡(u)=α−β​u2.\varphi(u)=au^{2}-bu^{3},\quad\text{and}\quad\psi(u)=\alpha-\beta u^{2}.

In this system (1.1)-(1.3), the variable u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) refers to the membrane electric potential of a neuronal cell, the variable v⁡(t,x)v(t,x) represents the transport rate of the ions of sodium and potassium through the fast ion channels and is called the spiking variable, while the variables w⁡(t,x)w(t,x) represents the transport rate across the neuronal cell membrane through slow channels of calcium and other ions and is called the bursting variable.

All the involved parameters are positive constants except c(=uR)∈ℝc\,(=u_{R})\in\mathbb{R}, which is a reference value of the membrane potential of a neuron cell. In the original model of ODE [39], a set of the typical parameters are

J=3.281,r=0.0021,S=4.0,q=r​S,c=−1.6,\displaystyle J=3.281,\;\;r=0.0021,\;\;S=4.0,\;\;q=rS,\;\;c=-1.6,
φ⁡(s)=3.0​s2−s3,ψ⁡(s)=1.0−5.0​s2.\displaystyle\varphi(s)=3.0s^{2}-s^{3},\;\;\psi(s)=1.0-5.0s^{2}.

We impose the homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions for the three components,

(1.5) ∂u∂ν​(t,x)=0,∂v∂ν​(t,x)=0,∂w∂ν​(t,x)=0,t>0,x∈∂Ω,\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}(t,x)=0,\;\;\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}(t,x)=0,\;\;\frac{\partial w}{\partial\nu}(t,x)=0,\quad t>0,\;x\in\partial\Omega,

and the initial conditions to be specified are denoted by

(1.6) u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x),v⁡(0,x)=v0​(x),w⁡(0,x)=w0​(x),x∈Ω.u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\quad v(0,x)=v_{0}(x),\quad w(0,x)=w_{0}(x),\quad x\in\Omega.

1.1. The Hindmarsh-Rose Model in ODE

In 1982-1984, J.L. Hindmarsh and R.M. Rose developed a mathematical model to describe neuronal activity and dynamics:

(1.7) d​ud​t=a​u2−b​u3+v−w+J,d​vd​t=α−β​u2−v,d​wd​t=q⁡(u−uR)−r​w.\begin{split}\frac{du}{dt}&=au^{2}-bu^{3}+v-w+J,\\ \frac{dv}{dt}&=\alpha-\beta u^{2}-v,\\ \frac{dw}{dt}&=q(u-u_{R})-rw.\end{split}

This neuron model was motivated by the discovery of neuronal cells in the pond snail Lymnaea which generated a burst after being depolarized by a short current pulse. This model characterizes the phenomena of synaptic bursting and especially chaotic bursting in a three-dimensional (u,v,w)(u,v,w) space.

Neuronal signals are short electrical pulses called spikes or action potential. Neurons often exhibit bursts of alternating phases of rapid firing spikes and then quiescence. Bursting constitutes a mechanism to modulate and set the pace for brain functionalities and to communicate signals with the neighbor neurons.

Bursting behaviors and patterns occur in a variety of excitable cells and bio-systems such as pituitary melanotropic gland, thalamic neurons, respiratory pacemaker neurons, and insulin-secreting pancreatic β\beta-cells, cf. [2, 4, 7, 15]. Neurons communicate and coordinate actions through synapses or diffusive coupling called gap junction in neuroscience. Synaptic coupling of neurons has to reach certain threshold for release of quantal vesicles and synchronization [8, 26, 28].

The mathematical analysis mainly using bifurcations together with numerical simulations of several models in ODEs on bursting behavior has been studied by many authors, cf. [1, 12, 18, 21, 24, 30, 29, 32, 33, 39].

The chaotic coupling exhibited in the simulations and analysis of this Hindmarsh-Rose model in ordinary differential equations shows more rapid synchronization and more effective regularization of neurons due to lower threshold than the synaptic coupling [32]. It was rigorously proved in [30, 39] that chaotic bursting solutions can be quickly synchronized and regularized when the coupling strength is large enough to topologically change the bifurcation diagram based on this Hindmarsh-Rose model, but the dynamics of chaotic bursting is highly complex.

It is known that Hodgkin-Huxley equations [16] (1952) provided a four-dimensional model for the dynamics of membrane potential taking into account of the sodium, potassium as well as leak ions current. It is a highly nonlinear system if without simplification assumptions. FitzHugh-Nagumo equations [13] (1961-1962) provided a two-dimensional model for an excitable neuron with the membrane potential and the current variable. This two-dimensional ODE model admits an exquisite phase plane analysis showing spikes excited by supra-threshold input pulses and sustained periodic spiking with refractory period, but due to the 2D nature FitzHugh-Nagumo equations exclude any chaotic solutions and chaotic dynamics so that no chaotic bursting can be generated.

The Hindmarsh-Rose equations (1.7) generate a significant mechanism for rapid firing and chaotic busting in neurodynamics. This model reflects possible lower down the neuron firing threshold and allows for spikes with varying interspike-interval. Therefore, this 3D model is a suitable choice for the investigation of both the regular bursting and the chaotic bursting when the parameters vary. The study of dynamical properties of the Hindmarsh-Rose equations exposes to a wide range of applications in neuroscience.

The rest of Section 1 presents the formulation of the system (1.1)-(1.6) and provides the relevant concepts and the recent results in [23] on the existence of global attractor for this diffusive Hindmarsh-Rise equations as well as the existing theory on exponential attractors. In Section 2, we shall prove a general theorem of the squeezing property for the abstract reaction-diffusion equation on a higher dimensional bounded domain. In Section 3, the main result on the existence of exponential attractor is established for the semiflow generated by the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations.

1.2. Formulation and Preliminaries

Neuron is a specialized biological cell in the brain and the central nervous system. In general, neurons are composed of the central cell body containing the nucleus and intracellular organelles, the dendrites, the axon, and the terminals. The dendrites are the short branches near the nucleus receiving incoming signals of voltage pulse and the axon is a long branch to propagate outgoing signals.

Neurons are immersed in aqueous chemical solutions consisting of different ions electrically charged. The cell membrane is the conductor along which the voltage signals travel. As pointed out in [19], neuron is a distributed dynamical system.

From physical and mathematical viewpoint, it is reasonable and useful to consider the Hindmarsh-Rose model in partial differential equations with the spatial variables xx involved, at least in ℝ1\mathbb{R}^{1}. Here in the abstract extent, we shall study the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations (1.1)-(1.3) on a bounded domain Ω\Omega of the space ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} and focus on the global asymptotic dynamics of the solutions.

We start with formulation of the aforementioned initial-boundary value problem of (1.1)–(1.6) into an abstract evolutionary equation. Define the Hilbert space H=[L2​(Ω)]3=L2​(Ω,ℝ3)H=[L^{2}(\Omega)]^{3}=L^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}) and the Sobolev space E=[H1​(Ω)]3=H1​(Ω,ℝ3)E=[H^{1}(\Omega)]^{3}=H^{1}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}). The norm and inner-product of HH or L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega) will be denoted by ∥⋅∥\|\,\cdot\,\| and ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\,\cdot,\cdot\,\rangle, respectively. The norm of EE will be denoted by ∥⋅∥E\|\,\cdot\,\|_{E}. The norm of Lp​(Ω)L^{p}(\Omega) or Lp​(Ω,ℝ3)L^{p}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}) will be dented by ∥⋅∥Lp\|\cdot\|_{L^{p}} if p≠2p\neq 2. We use |⋅||\,\cdot\,| to denote a vector norm in a Euclidean space.

The initial-boundary value problem (1.1)–(1.6) is formulated as an initial value problem of the evolutionary equation:

(1.8) ∂g∂t=Ag+f(g),t>0,g(0)=g0=(u0,v0,w0)∈H.\begin{split}&\frac{\partial g}{\partial t}=Ag+f(g),\quad t>0,\\[2.0pt] g&\,(0)=g_{0}=(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in H.\end{split}

Here the nonpositive self-adjoint operator

(1.9) A=(d1​Δ000d2​Δ000d3​Δ):D⁡(A)→H,A=\begin{pmatrix}d_{1}\Delta&0&0\\[3.0pt] 0&d_{2}\Delta&0\\[3.0pt] 0&0&d_{3}\Delta\end{pmatrix}:D(A)\rightarrow H,

where D⁡(A)={g∈H2​(Ω,ℝ3):∂g/∂ν=0}D(A)=\{g\in H^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}):\partial g/\partial\nu=0\} is the generator of an analytic C0C_{0}-semigroup {eA​t}t≥0\{e^{At}\}_{t\geq 0} on the Hilbert space HH due to the Lumer-Phillips theorem [27]. By the fact that H1​(Ω)↪L6​(Ω)H^{1}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^{6}(\Omega) is a continuous imbedding for space dimension n≤3n\leq 3 and by the Hölder inequality, there is a constant C0>0C_{0}>0 such that

‖φ⁡(u)‖≤C0​‖u‖L63and‖ψ⁡(u)‖≤C0​‖u‖L42for​u∈L6​(Ω).\|\varphi(u)\|\leq C_{0}\|u\|_{L^{6}}^{3}\quad\textup{and}\quad\|\psi(u)\|\leq C_{0}\|u\|_{L^{4}}^{2}\quad\textup{for}\;u\in L^{6}(\Omega).

Therefore, the nonlinear mapping

is a locally Lipschitz continuous mapping. We can simply write column vectors g⁡(t)g(t) as (u⁡(t,⋅),v⁡(t,⋅),w⁡(t,⋅))(u(t,\cdot),v(t,\cdot),w(t,\cdot)) and write g0=(u0,v0,w0)g_{0}=(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}). Definition 1.1.

A function g⁡(t,x),(t,x)∈[0,τ]×Ωg(t,x),(t,x)\in[0,\tau]\times\Omega, is called a weak solution to the initial value problem (1.8), if the following conditions are satisfied:

(i) dd​t​(g,ζ)=(A​g,ζ)+(f⁡(g),ζ)\frac{d}{dt}(g,\zeta)=(Ag,\zeta)+(f(g),\zeta) is satisfied for a.e. t∈[0,τ]t\in[0,\tau] and for any ζ∈E\zeta\in E;

In [23], the two authors and J. Su proved the following result on the existence of global solutions to the initial value problem (1.8).

Theorem 1.2.

For any given initial data g0=(u0,v0,w0)∈Hg_{0}=(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in H, there exists a unique global weak solution 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁g⁡(t,g0))=(u⁡(t),v⁡(t),w⁡(t)),t∈[0,∞)g(t,g_{0}))=(u(t),v(t),w(t)),\,t\in[0,\infty), of the initial value problem (1.8) for the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations (1.1)-(1.3), which continuously depends on the initial data and satisfies

(1.11) g∈C⁡([0,∞),H)∩C1​((0,∞),H)∩Ll​o​c2​([0,∞),E).g\in C([0,\infty);H)\cap C^{1}((0,\infty);H)\cap L_{loc}^{2}([0,\infty);E).

All the weak solution becomes a strong solution on the interval (0,∞)(0,\infty). The time-parametrized mapping {S⁡(t)​g0=g⁡(t,g0),t≥0}\{S(t)g_{0}=g(t,g_{0}),t\geq 0\} is called the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow.

1.3. Global Attractor and Exponential Attractor

We refer to [3, 5, 22, 25, 27, 31] for the basic concepts and results in the theory of infinite dimensional dynamical systems, including the few listed here for clarity.

Definition 1.3.

Let {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} be a semiflow on a Banach space 𝒳\mathscr{X}. A bounded set B0B_{0} of 𝒳\mathscr{X} is called an absorbing set for this semiflow, if for any given bounded subset B⊂𝒳B\subset\mathscr{X} there is a finite time T0≥0T_{0}\geq 0 depending on BB, such that S⁡(t)​B⊂B0S(t)B\subset B_{0} for all t≥T0t\geq T_{0}.

Definition 1.4 (Global Attractor).

A set 𝒜\mathscr{A} in a Banach space 𝒳\mathscr{X} is called a global attractor for a semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} on 𝒳\mathscr{X}, if the following two properties are satisfied:

(i) 𝒜\mathscr{A} is a nonempty, compact, and invariant set in the space 𝒳\mathscr{X}.

(ii) 𝒜\mathscr{A} attracts any given bounded set B⊂𝒳B\subset\mathscr{X} in the sense

dist𝒳​(S⁡(t)​B,𝒜)=supx∈Binfy∈𝒜‖S⁡(t)​x−y‖𝒳→0,as​t→∞.\text{dist}_{\mathscr{X}}(S(t)B,\mathscr{A})=\sup_{x\in B}\inf_{y\in\mathscr{A}}\|S(t)x-y\|_{\mathscr{X}}\to 0,\;\;\text{as}\;\;t\to\infty.

Global attractor characterizes qualitatively the longtime, asymptotic, and global dynamics of all the solution trajectories of a PDE system. As specified in [5, 25, 27, 31] as well as in [35, 36], global attractor is a depository (usually fractal finite-dimensional) of all the permanent regimes including chaotic structures of an infinite-dimensional dynamical system. Global dynamic patterns are also important in neural field and neural network theories [6, 12]. For the autocatalytic reaction-diffusion systems [35, 36, 37, 38], it is proved that global attractors exist.

Recently in [23], the two authors and J. Su proved the following theorems on the absorbing property of the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow and the existence of global attractor for the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations (1.8).

Theorem 1.5.

For any given bounded set B⊂HB\subset H, there exists a finite time TB>0T_{B}>0 such that for any initial state g0=(u0,v0,w0)∈Bg_{0}=(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in B, the weak solution g⁡(t)=S⁡(t)​g0=(u⁡(t),v⁡(t),w⁡(t))g(t)=S(t)g_{0}=(u(t),v(t),w(t)) of the initial value problem (1.8) uniquely exists for t∈[0,∞)t\in[0,\infty) and satisfies

(1.12) ‖(u⁡(t),v⁡(t),w⁡(t))‖E≤Q,for​t≥TB,\|(u(t),v(t),w(t))\|_{E}\leq Q,\quad\text{for}\;\;t\geq T_{B},

where Q>0Q>0 is a constant independent of any bounded set BB in HH, and the finite TB>0T_{B}>0 only depends on the bounded set BB.

We shall call the time-parametrized mapping {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow, which is a dynamical system on the space HH.

Theorem 1.6 (Global Attractor for Diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose Equations).

For any positive parameters d1,d2,d3,a,b,α,β,q,r,Jd_{1},d_{2},d_{3},a,b,\alpha,\beta,q,r,J and c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, there exists a global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} in the phase space H=L2​(Ω,ℝ3)H=L^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}) for the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} generated by the weak solutions of the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations (1.8). Moreover, the global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} is an (H,E)(H,E)-global attractor.

Global attractor for an infinite-dimensional dynamical systems generated by evolutionary PDE may exhibit slow rates and complicated behavior in attraction of solution trajectories. The notion of exponential attractor was introduced in [9].

Definition 1.7 (Exponential Attractor).

Suppose that XX is a Banach space and {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} is a semiflow on XX. A subset ℰ⊂X\mathscr{E}\subset X is called an exponential attractor for this semiflow if the following three conditions are satisfied:

1) ℰ\mathscr{E} is a compact in XX with a finite fractal dimension.

2) ℰ\mathscr{E} is positively invariant with respect to the semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} in the sense

S⁡(t)​ℰ⊂ℰfor all​t≥0.S(t)\mathscr{E}\subset\mathscr{E}\quad\text{for all}\;\;t\geq 0.

3) ℰ\mathscr{E} attracts all the solution trajectories exponentially with a uniform rate σ>0\sigma>0 in the sense that for any given bounded set B⊂XB\subset X there is a constant C⁡(B)>0C(B)>0 and

distX​(S⁡(t)​B,ℰ)≤C⁡(B)​e−σ​t,t≥0.\text{dist}_{X}(S(t)B,\mathscr{E})\leq C(B)e^{-\sigma t},\quad t\geq 0.

If there exists an exponential attractor ℰ\mathscr{E} (may not be unique) as well as a global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} for a semiflow in a Banach space XX, then it is always true that

𝒜⊂ℰ.\mathscr{A}\subset\mathscr{E}.

Consequently, the global attractor must have a finite fractal dimension as a subset of the exponential attractor.

There are two approaches in terms of sufficient conditions for construction of an exponential attractor. The first approach is the squeezing property which was introduced in the book [9] and expounded in [22]. The second approach is the compact smoothing property introduced by Efendiev-Miranville-Zelik [10, 11]. Conceptually, the two properties are essentially equivalent when the phase space is a Hilbert space. From the application viewpoint, the squeezing property fits more to the semilinear reaction-diffusion equations. The second approach has been exploited in proving the existence of exponential attractors for quasilinear reaction-diffusion systems [34].

The following definition of squeezing property [20, 22] for a mapping means that either the mapping (which can be s snapshot of a semiflow at any time t∗t^{*}) is a contraction or that higher modes are dominated by lower modes.

Definition 1.8 (Sqeezing Property).

Let HH be a Hilbert space and {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} be a semiflow on HH whose norm is ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|. Let S=S⁡(t∗)S=S(t^{*}) for some fixed t∗∈(0,∞)t^{*}\in(0,\infty). If there is a positively invariant set Z⊂HZ\subset H with respect to this semiflow and there is a constant 0<δ<10<\delta<1 and an orthogonal projection PP from HH onto a finite-dimensional subspace of P​H⊂HPH\subset H , such that either

‖S​u−S​v‖≤δ​‖u−v‖,for any​u,v∈Z,\|Su-Sv\|\leq\delta\|u-v\|,\quad\text{for any}\;u,v\in Z,

or

‖(I−P)​(S​u−S​v)‖≤‖P⁡(S​u−S​v)‖,for any​u,v∈Z,\|(I-P)(Su-Sv)\|\leq\|P(Su-Sv)\|,\quad\text{for any}\;u,v\in Z,

then we say that the mapping SS has the squeezing property and the affiliated semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} has the squeezing property on the set ZZ.

Definition 1.9 (Fractal Dimension).

The fractional dimension of a bounded subset ℳ\mathscr{M} in a Banach space is defined by

dimf​ℳ=lim supε→0+log⁡Nε​[ℳ]log⁡(1/ε)\text{dim}_{f}\,\mathscr{M}=\limsup_{\varepsilon\to 0^{+}}\frac{\log N_{\varepsilon}[\mathscr{M}]}{\log(1/\varepsilon)}

where Nε​[ℳ]N_{\varepsilon}[\mathscr{M}] is the infimum number of open balls with the radius ε\varepsilon for a covering of the set ℳ\mathscr{M}.

The following theorem states sufficient conditions for the existence of an exponential attractor with respect to a semiflow in a Hilbert space. Its proof is seen in [22, Theorems 4.4 and 4.5].

Theorem 1.10.

Let {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} be a semiflow on a Hilbert space HH with the following conditions satisfied:

1) The squeezing property is satisfied for S=S⁡(t∗)S=S(t^{*}) at some t∗>0t^{*}>0 on a nonempty,

compact, positively invariant, and absorbing set M⊂HM\subset H.

2) For all t∈[0,t∗]t\in[0,t^{*}], the mapping S⁡(t):M→MS(t):M\to M is Lipschitz continuous and the

Lipschitz constant K⁡(t):[0,t∗]→(0,∞)K(t):[0,t^{*}]\to(0,\infty) is a bounded function.

3) For any g∈Mg\in M, the mapping S⁡(⋅)​g:[0,t∗]→MS(\cdot)g:[0,t^{*}]\to M is Lipschitz continuous and

the Lipschitz constant L⁡(g):M→(0,∞)L(g):M\to(0,\infty) is a bounded function.

Then there exists an exponential attractor ℰ\mathscr{E} in the space HH for this semiflow. Moreover, for any θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1), the fractal dimension of the exponential attractor ℰ\mathscr{E} has the estimate

(1.13) dimF(ℰ)≤N​max⁡{1,log⁡(2​2​L/θ+1)−log⁡θ}\dim_{F}(\mathscr{E})\leq N\max\left\{1,\,\frac{\log(2\sqrt{2}L/\theta+1)}{-\log\theta}\right\}

where NN is the rank of the spectral projection associated with the squeezing property of the mapping S⁡(t∗)S(t^{*}) and LL is the Lipschitz constant of the mapping S⁡(t∗)S(t^{*}) on the positively invariant absorbing set MM.

2. Squeezing Property for Reaction-Diffusion Systems

The approach to proving the squeezing property for an evolutionary PDE is to study the difference of two solutions, w⁡(t)=g⁡(t)−h⁡(t)w(t)=g(t)-h(t), and conduct estimates to bound the time derivatives of the lower and higher modes, d​‖P​w‖/d​td\|Pw\|/dt and d​‖Q​w‖/d​td\|Qw\|/dt.

Consider a general system of reaction-diffusion equations in the form of an evolutionary equation on a real Hilbert space H=L2​(Ω,ℝd)H=L^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{d}), where the higher dimensional Ω⊂ℝd​(d≥3)\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}\,(d\geq 3), is a bounded Lipschitz domain,

(2.1) d​gd​t+𝒜​g=f⁡(g)\frac{dg}{dt}+\mathcal{A}g=f(g)

where f∈C1​(ℝd,ℝd)f\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R}^{d}) is a nonlinear vector function and the differential operator 𝒜:𝒟⁡(𝒜)→H\mathcal{A}:\mathscr{D}(\mathcal{A})\to H is a densely defined, nonnegative self-adjoint operator with compact resolvent so that its spectrum consists of a nonnegative sequence of the eigenvalues {λm}\{\lambda_{m}\} with finite multiplicities and λm→∞\lambda_{m}\to\infty as m→∞m\to\infty.

Assume that the weak solution g⁡(t)g(t) of the evolutionary equation (2.1) exists on the time interval [0,∞)[0,\infty) for any initial data g0∈Hg_{0}\in H, such that

(2.2) g∈C⁡([0,∞),H)∩Ll​o​c2​([0,∞),E)g\in C([0,\infty),H)\cap L^{2}_{loc}([0,\infty),E)

‖ξ⁡(t)‖≤‖ξ⁡(0)‖​eC​t,t≥0.\|\xi(t)\|\leq\|\xi(0)\|\,e^{Ct},\quad t\geq 0.

Substitute this inequality at t0t_{0} into (2.25) to obtain

‖q⁡(1)‖≤exp⁡(−λm2​Cm)​λm+Cm2​Cm​e2​‖ξ⁡(t0)‖≤exp⁡(−λm2​Cm)​λm+Cm2​Cm​e2+C​‖ξ⁡(0)‖.\begin{split}\|q(1)\|&\leq\exp\left(-\,\frac{\lambda_{m}}{2C_{m}}\right)\frac{\lambda_{m}+C_{m}}{2C_{m}}\;e^{2}\,\|\xi(t_{0})\|\\[5.0pt] &\leq\exp\left(-\,\frac{\lambda_{m}}{2C_{m}}\right)\frac{\lambda_{m}+C_{m}}{2C_{m}}\;e^{2+C}\,\|\xi(0)\|.\end{split}

Since ‖p⁡(1)‖<‖q⁡(1)‖\|p(1)\|<\|q(1)\|, we end up with

‖ξ⁡(1)‖≤2​exp⁡(−λm2​Cm)​λm+Cm2​Cm​e2+C​‖ξ⁡(0)‖.\|\xi(1)\|\leq\sqrt{2}\,\exp\left(-\,\frac{\lambda_{m}}{2C_{m}}\right)\frac{\lambda_{m}+C_{m}}{2C_{m}}\;e^{2+C}\|\xi(0)\|.

For mm sufficiently large, we can assert

0<δ=2​exp⁡(−λm2​Cm)​λm+Cm2​Cm​e2+2​C=2​(λm2​C​(λm12+1)+12)​exp⁡(−λm2​C​(λm12+1))​e2+2​C<1.\begin{split}0<\delta&=\sqrt{2}\,\exp\left(-\,\frac{\lambda_{m}}{2C_{m}}\right)\frac{\lambda_{m}+C_{m}}{2C_{m}}\;e^{2+2C}\\ &=\sqrt{2}\,\left(\frac{\lambda_{m}}{2C(\lambda_{m}^{\frac{1}{2}}+1)}+\frac{1}{2}\right)\exp\left(-\,\frac{\lambda_{m}}{2C(\lambda_{m}^{\frac{1}{2}}+1)}\right)e^{2+2C}<1.\end{split}

We have proved that

(2.27) ‖S​g0−S​h0‖=‖ξ⁡(1)‖≤δ|ξ⁡(0)|=δ​‖g0−h0‖,for any​g0,h0∈M.\|Sg_{0}-Sh_{0}\|=\|\xi(1)\|\leq\delta\|\xi(0)\|=\delta\|g_{0}-h_{0}\|,\quad\text{for any}\;\,g_{0},h_{0}\in M.

Finally (2.16) and (2.27) show that, in any case as we have treated in Step 2 and Step 3, if the spectral number mm of the finite-rank orthogonal projection PmP_{m} on the space HH is chosen to be large enough, then the squeezing property holds for the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} generated by the equation (2.1) on this compact, positively invariant and bounded set M⊂HM\subset H. The proof is completed. ∎

3. The Existence of Exponential Attractor

In this section, we shall prove the main result on the existence of an exponential attractor for the solution semiflow of the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations.

We start with the squeezing property stated Theorem 2.1 and check its two conditions (2.3) and (2.4) are satisfied by the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow.

Lemma 3.1.

Under the same assumptions as in Theorem 1.6, the Nemytskii operator ff defined by (1.10) satisfies the EE to HH Lipschitz condition

(3.1) ‖f⁡(g)−f⁡(g~)‖H≤CE​(M)​‖g−g~‖E,for any​g,g~∈M,\|f(g)-f(\tilde{g})\|_{H}\leq C_{E}(M)\|g-\tilde{g}\|_{E},\quad\text{for any}\;\;g,\tilde{g}\in M,

on any given positively invariant and bounded set M⊂EM\subset E, where CE​(M)>0C_{E}(M)>0 is a constant only depending on MM. Moreover, ff satisfies the monotone property that there exists a constant C∗>0C^{*}>0 independent of MM such that

(3.2) ⟨f⁡(g)−f⁡(g~),g−g~⟩≤C∗​‖g−g~‖2,for any​g,g~∈M.\langle f(g)-f(\tilde{g}),g-\tilde{g}\rangle\leq C^{*}\|g-\tilde{g}\|^{2},\quad\text{for any}\;\;g,\,\tilde{g}\in M.

where we used

a⁡(u⁡(x)+v⁡(x))≤b4​(u2​(x)+u~2​(x))+2​a2b.a(u(x)+v(x))\leq\frac{b}{4}(u^{2}(x)+\tilde{u}^{2}(x))+\frac{2a^{2}}{b}.

For the second component f2f_{2}, we do the estimate

(3.4) ⟨f2​(g)−f2​(g~),v−v~⟩=⟨f2​(u,v,w)−f2​(u~,v~,w~),v−v~⟩≤⟨ψ⁡(u)−ψ⁡(u~),v−v~⟩+‖v−v~‖2=β​∫Ω(u⁡(x)−u~​(x))​(u⁡(x)+u~​(x))​(v⁡(x)−v~​(x))​dx+‖v−v~‖2≤b8​∫Ω|u⁡(x)−u~​(x)|2​|u⁡(x)+u~​(x)|2​dx+2​β2b​‖v−v~‖2+‖v−v~‖2≤b4​∫Ω|u⁡(x)−u~​(x)|2​(u2​(x)+u~2​(x))​dx+(1+2​β2b)​‖v−v~‖2.\begin{split}&\langle f_{2}(g)-f_{2}(\tilde{g}),v-\tilde{v}\rangle=\langle f_{2}(u,v,w)-f_{2}(\tilde{u},\tilde{v},\tilde{w}),v-\tilde{v}\rangle\\[7.0pt] \leq&\,\langle\psi(u)-\psi(\tilde{u}),v-\tilde{v}\rangle+\|v-\tilde{v}\|^{2}\\ =&\,\beta\int_{\Omega}(u(x)-\tilde{u}(x))(u(x)+\tilde{u}(x))(v(x)-\tilde{v}(x))\,dx+\|v-\tilde{v}\|^{2}\\ \leq&\,\frac{b}{8}\int_{\Omega}|u(x)-\tilde{u}(x)|^{2}|u(x)+\tilde{u}(x)|^{2}\,dx+\frac{2\beta^{2}}{b}\|v-\tilde{v}\|^{2}+\|v-\tilde{v}\|^{2}\\ \leq&\,\frac{b}{4}\int_{\Omega}|u(x)-\tilde{u}(x)|^{2}(u^{2}(x)+\tilde{u}^{2}(x))\,dx+\left(1+\frac{2\beta^{2}}{b}\right)\|v-\tilde{v}\|^{2}.\end{split}

For the third component f3f_{3}, we have

(3.5) ⟨f3​(g)−f3​(g~),w−w~⟩=⟨f3​(u,v,w)−f3​(u~,v~,w~),w−w~⟩≤q​‖u−u~‖​‖w−w~‖+r​‖w−w~‖2≤q​‖u−u~‖2+(q+r)​‖w−w~‖2.\begin{split}&\langle f_{3}(g)-f_{3}(\tilde{g}),w-\tilde{w}\rangle=\langle f_{3}(u,v,w)-f_{3}(\tilde{u},\tilde{v},\tilde{w}),w-\tilde{w}\rangle\\[3.0pt] \leq&\,q\|u-\tilde{u}\|\|w-\tilde{w}\|+r\|w-\tilde{w}\|^{2}\leq q\|u-\tilde{u}\|^{2}+(q+r)\|w-\tilde{w}\|^{2}.\end{split}

Summing up (3.3), (3.4) and (3.5) with two integral terms on the right-hand sides being cancelled out, we obtain

(3.6) ⟨f⁡(g)−f⁡(g~),g−g~⟩=⟨f1​(g)−f1​(g~),u−u~⟩+⟨f2​(g)−f2​(g~),v−v~⟩+⟨f3​(g)−f3​(g~),w−w~⟩≤(1+2​a2b)​‖u−u~‖2+‖v−v~‖2+‖w−w~‖2+(1+2​β2b)​‖v−v~‖2+q​‖u−u~‖2+(q+r)​‖w−w~‖2=(1+q+2​a2b)​‖u−u~‖2+(2+2​β2b)​‖v−v~‖2+(1+q+r)​‖w−w~‖2≤C∗​(‖u−u~‖2+‖v−v~‖2+‖w−w~‖2)=C∗​‖g−g~‖2.\begin{split}&\langle f(g)-f(\tilde{g}),g-\tilde{g}\rangle=\langle f_{1}(g)-f_{1}(\tilde{g}),u-\tilde{u}\rangle\\[7.0pt] +&\,\langle f_{2}(g)-f_{2}(\tilde{g}),v-\tilde{v}\rangle+\langle f_{3}(g)-f_{3}(\tilde{g}),w-\tilde{w}\rangle\\ \leq&\,\left(1+\frac{2a^{2}}{b}\right)\|u-\tilde{u}\|^{2}+\|v-\tilde{v}\|^{2}+\|w-\tilde{w}\|^{2}\\ +&\,\left(1+\frac{2\beta^{2}}{b}\right)\|v-\tilde{v}\|^{2}+q\|u-\tilde{u}\|^{2}+(q+r)\|w-\tilde{w}\|^{2}\\ =&\,\left(1+q+\frac{2a^{2}}{b}\right)\|u-\tilde{u}\|^{2}+\left(2+\frac{2\beta^{2}}{b}\right)\|v-\tilde{v}\|^{2}+(1+q+r)\|w-\tilde{w}\|^{2}\\ \leq&\,C^{*}\,(\|u-\tilde{u}\|^{2}+\|v-\tilde{v}\|^{2}+\|w-\tilde{w}\|^{2})=C^{*}\,\|g-\tilde{g}\|^{2}.\end{split}

Thus the inequality (3.2) is satisfied by ff on the set MM with a uniform constant

(3.7) C∗=max⁡{1+q+2​a2b, 2+2​β2b, 1+q+r}.C^{*}=\max\left\{1+q+\frac{2a^{2}}{b},\,2+\frac{2\beta^{2}}{b},\,1+q+r\right\}.

Next we prove the EE to HH Lipschitz condition (3.1) of the Nemytskii operator ff. Then

(3.8) ∥f(g)−f(g~)∥2H=∥f1(g)−f1(g~)∥2+∥f2(g)−f2(g~)∥2+∥f3(g)−f3(g~)∥2≤(a​‖u2−u~2‖+b​‖u3−u~3‖+‖v−v~‖+‖w−w~‖)2+(β​‖u2−u~2‖+‖v−v~‖)2+(q​‖u−u~‖+r​‖w−w~‖)2≤ 4​(a2​‖u2−u~2‖2+b2​‖u3−u~3‖2+‖v−v~‖2+‖w−w~‖2)+ 2​(β2​‖u2−u~2‖2+‖v−v~‖2)+2​(q2​‖u−u~‖2+r2​‖w−w~‖2)=(4​a2+2​β2)​‖u2−u~2‖2+4​b2​‖u3−u~3‖2+2​q2​‖u−u~‖2+ 6​‖v−v~‖2+(4+2​r2)​‖w−w~‖2.\begin{split}\|f(g)-&\,f(\tilde{g})\|^{2}_{H}=\|f_{1}(g)-f_{1}(\tilde{g})\|^{2}+\|f_{2}(g)-f_{2}(\tilde{g})\|^{2}+\|f_{3}(g)-f_{3}(\tilde{g})\|^{2}\\[3.0pt] \leq&\,(a\|u^{2}-\tilde{u}^{2}\|+b\|u^{3}-\tilde{u}^{3}\|+\|v-\tilde{v}\|+\|w-\tilde{w}\|)^{2}\\[3.0pt] +&\,(\beta\|u^{2}-\tilde{u}^{2}\|+\|v-\tilde{v}\|)^{2}+(q\|u-\tilde{u}\|+r\|w-\tilde{w}\|)^{2}\\[2.0pt] \leq&\,4(a^{2}\|u^{2}-\tilde{u}^{2}\|^{2}+b^{2}\|u^{3}-\tilde{u}^{3}\|^{2}+\|v-\tilde{v}\|^{2}+\|w-\tilde{w}\|^{2})\\[3.0pt] +&\,2(\beta^{2}\|u^{2}-\tilde{u}^{2}\|^{2}+\|v-\tilde{v}\|^{2})+2(q^{2}\|u-\tilde{u}\|^{2}+r^{2}\|w-\tilde{w}\|^{2})\\[3.0pt] =&\,(4a^{2}+2\beta^{2})\|u^{2}-\tilde{u}^{2}\|^{2}+4b^{2}\|u^{3}-\tilde{u}^{3}\|^{2}+2q^{2}\|u-\tilde{u}\|^{2}\\[3.0pt] +&\,6\|v-\tilde{v}\|^{2}+(4+2r^{2})\|w-\tilde{w}\|^{2}.\end{split}

Note that Hölder inequality implies that

‖u2−u~2‖2=\displaystyle\|u^{2}-\tilde{u}^{2}\|^{2}= ‖(u−u~)​(u+u~)‖2=∫Ω|u⁡(x)−u~​(x)|2​|u⁡(x)+u~​(x)|2​𝑑x\displaystyle\,\|(u-\tilde{u})(u+\tilde{u})\|^{2}=\int_{\Omega}|u(x)-\tilde{u}(x)|^{2}|u(x)+\tilde{u}(x)|^{2}\,dx
≤\displaystyle\leq ‖u−u~‖L42​‖u+u~‖L42≤4​δ12​N12​‖u−u~‖H1​(Ω)2\displaystyle\,\|u-\tilde{u}\|_{L^{4}}^{2}\|u+\tilde{u}\|_{L^{4}}^{2}\leq 4\,\delta_{1}^{2}N_{1}^{2}\|u-\tilde{u}\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)}^{2}

which shows that (3.1) is valid with the constant CE​(M)>0C_{E}(M)>0 given by

Now we prove the existence of an exponential attractor for the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} generated by the Hindmarsh-Rose evolutionary equation (1.8)

Theorem 3.2.

Under the same assumptions as in Theorem 1.6, there exists an exponential attractor ℰ\mathscr{E} in the space H=L2​(Ω,ℝ3)H=L^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}) for the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} generated by the weak solutions of the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations (1.8).

Proof.

We shall go through the following steps to check all the three conditions stated in Theorem 1.10.

Step 1. First we show that there exists a compact, positively invariant and absorbing set M⊂HM\subset H for the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} such that (2.3) and (2.4) are satisfied. Then according to Theorem 2.1 the squeezing property is satisfied for the mapping S⁡(t∗)S(t^{*}) at t∗=1t^{*}=1 on this set MM.

Theorem 1.5 has shown that the closed and bounded ball BE​(Q)B_{E}(Q) centered at the origin with radius Q>0Q>0 in the space E=H1​(Ω,ℝ3)E=H^{1}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}) is an absorbing set for this semiflow. We can easily verify that the set

(3.10) M=⋃0≤t≤T∗S⁡(t)​BE​(Q)¯M=\overline{\bigcup_{0\leq t\leq T^{*}}S(t)B_{E}(Q)}

is a compact, positively invariant and absorbing set in the space HH for this semiflow, where T∗=T∗​(BE​(Q))T^{*}=T^{*}(B_{E}(Q)) is the permanently entering time for the solution trajectories starting from the ball BE​(Q)B_{E}(Q) into itself, as indicated in (1.12). The compactness of MM in HH is inferred by the boundedness of MM in the space EE and the compact embedding E↪HE\hookrightarrow H so that the cylinder [0,T∗]×BE​(Q)[0,T^{*}]\times B_{E}(Q) is a compact set in ℝ×H\mathbb{R}\times H and by the fact that the function

(3.11) γ⁡(t,g)=S⁡(t)​g​is continuous on​[0,T∗]×BE​(Q).\gamma(t,g)=S(t)g\,\;\text{is continuous on}\,\;[0,T^{*}]\times B_{E}(Q).

In Lemma 3.1 it has been shown that the nonlinear mapping f⁡(g)f(g) given in (1.10) satisfies the Lipschitz continuous condition (2.3) and the monotone condition (2.4) on this set MM given in (3.10). Moreover by the continuity of the functions γ⁡(t,g)\gamma(t,g) in (3.11), we see that

(3.12) G=max⁡{‖γ⁡(t,g)‖E:(t,g)∈[0,T∗]×BE​(Q)}<∞.G=\max\{\|\gamma(t,g)\|_{E}:(t,g)\in[0,T^{*}]\times B_{E}(Q)\}<\infty.

Thus we can apply Theorem 2.1 with its proof to confirm that the squeezing property is satisfied by the mapping S⁡(t∗)S(t^{*}) at t∗=1t^{*}=1 so that the squeezing property is satisfied by the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} on this set MM in HH. Therefore, the first condition in Theorem 1.10 is satisfied by the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow.

Step 2. Next we show that, for the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow and for any t∈[0,t∗]=[0,1]t\in[0,t^{*}]=[0,1], the mapping S⁡(t):M→MS(t):M\to M is Lipschitz continuous in HH and the associated Lipschitz constant K⁡(t):[0,1]→(0,∞)K(t):[0,1]\to(0,\infty) is a bounded function.

For this purpose, consider any two g0=(u0,v0,w0),g~0=(u~0,v~0,w~0)∈Mg_{0}=(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}),\tilde{g}_{0}=(\tilde{u}_{0},\tilde{v}_{0},\tilde{w}_{0})\in M and the solutions g⁡(t)=S⁡(t)​g0g(t)=S(t)g_{0} and g~​(t)=S​(t)​g~0\tilde{g}(t)=S(t)\tilde{g}_{0} for t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]. Then h​(t)=g​(t)−g~​(t)h(t)=g(t)-\tilde{g}(t) satisfies the equation

(3.13) d​hd​t=Ah+f(g)−f(g~),t>0,h⁡(0)=h0=g0−g~0.\begin{split}\frac{dh}{dt}&\,=Ah+f(g)-f(\tilde{g}),\quad t>0,\\ &h(0)=h_{0}=g_{0}-\tilde{g}_{0}.\end{split}

For any given g0∈Mg_{0}\in M, since the weak solution S⁡(t)​g0,t≥0S(t)g_{0},t\geq 0, is a mild solution for the evolutionary equation (1.8), we have

(3.20) S⁡(t)​g0=eA​t​g0+∫0teA⁡(t−s)​f​(g⁡(s,g0))​𝑑t,t≥0,S(t)g_{0}=e^{At}g_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}e^{A(t-s)}f(g(s,g_{0}))\,dt,\quad t\geq 0,

where the operator AA and the nonlinear mapping ff are defined in (1.9) and (1.10), respectively. A fundamental theorem on sectorial operators [27, Theorem 37.5] shows that the operator function eA​t:[0,∞)→ℒ⁡(H)e^{At}:[0,\infty)\to\mathcal{L}(H) is uniformly Lipschitz continuous. Actually, the spectral expansion of eA​te^{At} shows

where {−λk}k=1∞\{-\lambda_{k}\}_{k=1}^{\infty}, with 0≤λk→∞0\leq\lambda_{k}\to\infty as k→∞k\to\infty, is the set of all the eigenvalues (repeated to the respective multiplicities) of A:D⁡(A)→HA:D(A)\to H, and {ek}k=1∞\{e_{k}\}_{k=1}^{\infty} with A​ek=−λk​ekAe_{k}=-\lambda_{k}e_{k} is the complete set of the orthonormal eigenvectors of AA. (3.21) ‖eA​t​g0−eA​τ​g0‖2=∑k=1∞|e−λk​(t−τ)|2​|⟨g0,ek⟩|2=∑k=1∞|e−ζk|2​λk​|t−τ|​|⟨g0,ek⟩|2​(where​ 0≤λk​τ≤ζk≤λk​t)≤|t−τ|​‖∇g0‖2≤|t−τ|​‖g0‖E2≤G2​|t−τ|.\begin{split}&\|e^{At}g_{0}-e^{A\tau}g_{0}\|^{2}=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\,|e^{-\lambda_{k}(t-\tau)}|^{2}|\langle g_{0},e_{k}\rangle|^{2}\\ =&\,\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\,|e^{-\zeta_{k}}|^{2}\lambda_{k}|t-\tau||\langle g_{0},e_{k}\rangle|^{2}\;\;(\text{where}\;0\leq\lambda_{k}\tau\leq\zeta_{k}\leq\lambda_{k}t)\\[5.0pt] \leq&\,|t-\tau|\|\nabla g_{0}\|^{2}\leq|t-\tau|\|g_{0}\|_{E}^{2}\leq G^{2}|t-\tau|.\end{split}

L⁡(M)=(1+CE​(M))​G2+(J+α+q​|c|).L(M)=(1+C_{E}(M))G^{2}+(J+\alpha+q|c|).

Then clearly the claim in Step 3 is proved.

Since we have proved that all the three conditions in Theorem 1.10 are satisfied by the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow, there exists an exponential attractor ℰ\mathscr{E} in the space HH for this Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow. The proof is completed. ∎

The existence of an exponential attractor as well as the squeezing property have the following meaningful corollaries on the finite fractal dimensionality of the global attractor shown in [23] and on the determining modes.

Corollary 3.3.

The global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} of the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow has a finite fractal dimension

(3.23) dimF(𝒜)≤N​max⁡{1,log⁡(2​2​K/θ+1)−log⁡θ},θ∈(0,1),\dim_{F}(\mathscr{A})\leq N\max\left\{1,\frac{\log(2\sqrt{2}K/\theta+1)}{-\log\theta}\right\},\quad\theta\in(0,1),

where NN is the rank of the spectral projection associated with the squeezing property of the mapping S⁡(1)S(1) and KK is the Lipschitz constant of the mapping S⁡(1)S(1) on the compact, positively invariant, absorbing set MM.

Proof.

This result is simply implied by the inclusion of the global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} in the exponential attractor ℰ\mathscr{E},

𝒜⊂ℰ\mathscr{A}\subset\mathscr{E}

because limt→∞d​i​s​tH​(S⁡(t)​𝒜,ℰ)=d​i​s​tH​(𝒜,ℰ)=0\lim_{t\to\infty}dist_{H}(S(t)\mathscr{A},\mathscr{E})=dist_{H}(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{E})=0, and that by definition the exponential attractor ℰ\mathscr{E} has a finite fractal dimension. The estimate (3.23) follows from Theorem 1.10. ∎

Corollary 3.4.

Under the same assumptions as in Theorem 1.6, the orthogonal projection of the trajectories in the global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} on the finite dimensional subspace P​HPH of the low modes is determining in the sense that, for two trajectories g⁡(t)g(t) and g~​(t)\tilde{g}(t) in 𝒜\mathscr{A}, if

‖P​g​(t)−P​g~​(t)‖H→0,as​t→∞,\|Pg(t)-P\tilde{g}(t)\|_{H}\to 0,\quad\text{as}\;\;t\to\infty,

then

‖g⁡(t)−g~​(t)‖H→0,as​t→∞.\|g(t)-\tilde{g}(t)\|_{H}\to 0,\quad\text{as}\;\;t\to\infty.

Here the finite-rank orthogonal projection PP is affiliated with the corresponding squeezing property of the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow.

This Corollary 3.4 is a consequence of the squeezing property of the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow shown in Theorem 3.2 above and Theorem 14.3 in [25].
